cases.label: A

fact_coverage.evidence: Abstract: "General matrix multiplications in DNN training" expose "uneven matrix dimensions and unstructured zeros"; introduction 1 explains stranded multipliers and useless execution slots.

Introduction 2: "logical row of multipliers" forms Flex-DPEs; "Benes distribution fabric supports operand multicast" and FAN routes partial sums so "independently sized dot products can share the reduction fabric."

Introduction 2: "A bitmap identifies zero positions and guides placement of useful operands"; Flex-DPEs compose into a Flex-DPU, and evaluation reports the better weight-stationary/input-stationary mapping.

Introduction 3 supplies "GNMT, Transformer, NCF, and DeepBench," a "cycle-based analytical model," "SCALE-sim," "16,384 PEs," and all six named sparse baselines. Abstract explicitly says "kernel comparisons, not full training results."

Introduction 3: "5.7× speedup over TPU-like systolic designs on sparse irregular workloads and approximately 3× over the compared sparse accelerators"; preceding sentence says these were extended to GEMMs with alternative orientations and sparsity placements explored.

Introduction 3: "Post-layout compute-array results at 28 nm and 500 MHz, using BF16 multiplication and FP32 addition," followed by SIGMA 65.10 mm²/22.33 W versus systolic 47.27 mm²/12.25 W; "large SRAMs are excluded."

Introduction 3 gives "37.7% area increase" and explains Eyeriss v2 winning "two GEMMs by retaining both operands locally while SIGMA streams one repeatedly"; abstract expressly retains "streaming sparsity, and bandwidth" as limits.

cases.rationale: Specific useful-work problem leads to flexible distribution/reduction, then scoped model and physical-cost evidence. All fact groups are represented without enlarged result scope. The 206-word abstract and three introduction paragraphs meet form constraints. Repetition of results and qualifications makes the evaluation paragraph somewhat dense.

cases.label: B

fact_coverage.evidence: Introduction 1 explains ordinary loads/stores to byte-addressable nonvolatile storage alongside volatile DRAM, crash recovery, permissible update order, and epochs grouping persistent stores "between ordering points."

Introduction 2: "WHISPER assembles ten applications spanning direct persistence, transactional libraries, and file-system access"; programs are adapted for recovery/instrumented, with persistent-access traces extracted by Eliza. These cover the key suite categories, though individual example systems are not enumerated.
Introduction 2 reports 5–50 epochs with Echo/N-store TPC-C exceptions above a hundred, common same-thread conflicts and uncommon cross-thread conflicts that "remain possible."
Introduction 2 limits "3.54% of memory accesses" to the "simulated application subset" and connects it to the mix dominated by volatile traffic.

Introduction 2 gives ofence closing an epoch "without demanding synchronous durability," dfence waiting at transaction completion, per-thread buffers retaining updates/multiple versions and dependency metadata recording necessary order.
Introduction 3: gem5 full-system Linux, four-core out-of-order x86, subset to completion, 32-entry buffers per hardware thread and flushing at 16 entries.

Introduction 3 gives HOPS without persistent write queues, 24.3% over x86-64 clwb/sfence with durability at NVM, 10% over the x86-64 Persistent Write Queue configuration and an ideal reference explicitly "not crash-consistent."
Introduction 3 retains buffers/versions/metadata/cache-coherence costs, unestablished aggregate chip-area/power, cross-thread conflict handling and conservative dependency false positives.

cases.rationale: Application behavior supports the separation of ordering and completion, with fence semantics and retained versions explaining the effect. Numerical gains preserve baseline configurations and simulated-subset scope. The 204-word abstract and three paragraphs satisfy form constraints. The conclusion partly restates qualifications already established, but the progression remains clear.

cases.label: A

fact_coverage.evidence: Abstract and introduction 1 identify a deployed inference TPU, six production MLP/CNN/LSTM models covering 95% of the provider's inference demand "at the time," versus contemporary Haswell/K80.

Introduction 2 identifies a host-controlled PCIe inference coprocessor with a dense systolic unit, 65,536 MACs, 8-bit integer operands, software-managed Unified Buffer and simple deterministic execution.
Introduction 2 gives peak 92 trillion operations/s, 24 MiB Unified Buffer, 4 MiB accumulators and no dedicated sparse-operation support; it distinguishes peak rate from sustained throughput.

Introduction 1 explains batching/tail-latency tradeoffs and MLP0's 7 ms 99th-percentile limit; introduction 3 enforces latency limits/includes host overhead and distinguishes quantized TPU from floating-point CPU/GPU.
Introduction 3 gives Haswell 14.5× geometric/29.2× weighted and K80 13.2×/15.3×, with latency limits and host overhead included.
Introduction 3 scopes 17–34× Haswell and 14–16× K80 to complete-server performance/W, distinguishes higher incremental ratios subtracting host power, and says purchase price/TCO are undisclosed.
Introduction 2 links roofline/counters to MLP/LSTM memory limits and low utilization despite relative throughput; introduction 3 gives CNN0 at 10% offered load consuming 88% full-load power.
Introduction 3 calls higher-bandwidth alternatives "predictions rather than deployed measurements"; introduction 1 identifies the baselines as contemporary.

cases.rationale: Strong service-constrained argument and carefully interpreted throughput/power evidence preserve workload, precision, aggregation and host boundaries. The mechanism describes the architecture and bandwidth constraint but says less about how systolic/deterministic execution itself yields specialization benefits. Abstract is 203 words with exactly three introduction paragraphs; the last paragraph is dense with distinct qualifications.

cases.label: B

fact_coverage.evidence: Introduction 1 defines when/where tensor computations execute and connects operator dimensions, spatial/temporal reuse, communication, buffers and bandwidth; it says stationary labels are insufficient for complete mappings.

Introduction 2 explains TemporalMap/SpatialMap/Cluster, hierarchical reuse/communication analysis and estimates of runtime, activity counts, energy, buffers and utilization from workload/mapping/hardware.

Introduction 1 requires suitable multicast/reduction hardware and buffer capacity and notes extra PEs/buffering may not help bandwidth limits; introduction 2 combines activities with component energy and synthesized area/power costs.
Introduction 3 gives 64-PE MAERI RTL on VGG16 plus reported Eyeriss on AlexNet, average absolute runtime error within 3.9%, expressly excluding all-dataflow bounds and energy-error validation.
Introduction 3 states modeled five-style/five-DNN operator comparisons, operator-dependent preferred mappings and potential runtime/energy reductions of 37%/10% in that case study.

Introduction 2 varies PEs, local/shared buffers and NoC bandwidth under area/power constraints, pruning through cost lower bounds; introduction 3 scopes 3,936,256 explored/175,861 valid/12.20 minutes to KC-P/VGG16-CONV2. Abstract says explored points are not full simulations.
Introduction 3 gives Intel i7-8700K, 32 GB, synthesized 28 nm component costs, 16 mm²/450 mW search constraints and explicitly distinguishes these from tool overhead.

Introduction 3 identifies an analytical exploration tool with automatic tuning/RTL generation future capabilities; introduction 2 distinguishes abstract comparisons from measurements of manufactured accelerators.

cases.rationale: The argument connects mapping precision to realizable reuse and resource needs; mechanism and evidence cover the analytic model, component costs, bounded runtime validation and search pruning. Neither modeled gains nor future capabilities become deployed claims. The 209-word abstract and three paragraphs satisfy form constraints; repeated scope caveats add some density.
